old: Halogens are more electronegative than carbon, so the C–X bond is polar: the carbon carries $\delta+$ and the halogen $\delta-$. This makes the carbon an electrophilic site for nucleophiles. Down the group the halogen gets larger, so C–X bond length increases ($C-F < C-Cl < C-Br < C-I$) and bond enthalpy decreases. C–I is therefore the weakest bond, and iodides are the most reactive alkyl halides. Dipole moment order is $CH_3Cl > CH_3F > CH_3Br > CH_3I$; $CH_3F$ is lower than $CH_3Cl$ because its very short bond outweighs its higher charge separation. In haloarenes the C–X bond is shorter and stronger than in haloalkanes for four reasons: the carbon is $sp^2$ hybridised, resonance gives the bond partial double-bond character, the phenyl cation is unstable, and the electron-rich ring repels incoming nucleophiles. Haloarenes therefore resist nucleophilic substitution unless electron-withdrawing groups such as $-NO_2$ sit at the ortho or para positions.
